transcript.sourceText: A natural monopoly has declining average cost across the relevant market range, making one large producer less costly than several small firms. The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC. Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.
transcript.text: A natural monopoly has declining average cost across the relevant market range, making one large producer less costly than several small firms. The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC. Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P equals M C efficiency benchmark. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

WATCH OUT

runs.text: Do not confuse allocative efficiency with break even. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC. Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.

WORKED EXAMPLE: REGULATING A NATURAL MONOPOLY

Marginal-cost pricing sets demand equal to MC, which the graph shows at 140 units and $10. ATC there is about $15, so the regulated firm would lose about ($15 - $10) x 140 = $700. Average-cost pricing near 115 units and $16 avoids that loss but leaves price above marginal cost.
